rendered_text:
=== Divorce ===

Topic: Divorce (divorce) — forced by request

--- Christianity — discouraged ---
What God has joined, man should not put asunder: Jesus treats the Mosaic divorce provision as a concession to hardness of heart, not the design. The exception clause for unfaithfulness and Paul's provision for abandonment ground the historic grounds for separation, and the communions divide over remarriage — from Catholic indissolubility to broader Protestant and Orthodox accommodation.
  • Jesus recalls marriage to its beginning and names remarriage after groundless divorce adultery. [C1]
      “He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so. And I say unto you, Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery: and whoso marrieth her which is put away doth commit adultery.”
      — Matthew 19:8–9 — The Holy Bible, King James Version, trans. the King James translators (1611)
      Context: Jesus treats the Mosaic divorce provision as concession, not ideal, while the exception clause became the crux of Christian divorce doctrine and its denominational splits.
  • Paul releases the believer abandoned by an unbelieving spouse, showing the bond can be dissolved by desertion. [C2]
      “But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace.”
      — 1 Corinthians 7:15 — The Holy Bible, King James Version, trans. the King James translators (1611)
      Context: The Pauline concession for marriages abandoned by an unbelieving spouse; churches differ over how far this 'privilege' extends the grounds for divorce.
  Note: Catholic doctrine holds sacramental marriage indissoluble (annulment aside); Orthodoxy tolerates penitential remarriage; most Protestant bodies accept divorce for cause — one of the sharpest intra-Christian divides.
  Further reading:
      - David Instone-Brewer, “Divorce and Remarriage in the Bible” (2002) [book]

--- Islam — permitted ---
Divorce is lawful in Islam and regulated in detail: staged pronouncements, waiting periods, arbitration from both families first, and the standing command that a wife be retained in honour or released in kindness. A well-known hadith calls it the most disliked of permitted things — the law's permission is real, and so is its reluctance.
  • The divorce verses regulate rather than forbid, insisting on honour or kindness at every stage. [C3]
      “Divorce must be pronounced twice and then (a woman) must be retained in honour or released in kindness.”
      — Qur'an 2:229 — The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall (1930)
      Context: Divorce is lawful but procedurally braked: staged pronouncements, waiting periods, and the standing command of honour or kindness govern the release.
  • Family arbitration is prescribed before dissolution, structuring repair before release. [C4]
      “And if ye fear a breach between them twain (the man and wife), appoint an arbiter from his folk and an arbiter from her folk. If they desire amendment Allah will make them of one mind. Lo! Allah is ever Knower, Aware.”
      — Qur'an 4:35 — The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall (1930)
      Context: Arbitration from both families is prescribed before the bond is dissolved; ending a marriage is preceded by structured attempts at repair.
  Note: Schools differ over unilateral talaq, judicial divorce (khul'), and modern statutory reform; the 'most hateful of permitted things' hadith frames all of them.
  Further reading:
      - Judith E. Tucker, “Women, Family, and Gender in Islamic Law” (2008) [book]

--- Judaism — permitted ---
The Torah legislates divorce rather than forbidding it: the get, written and delivered, dissolves the bond, and Hillel's school allowed it on broad grounds. Yet the tractate that regulates it closes with the altar shedding tears for the divorce of the wife of one's youth. Divorce is lawful, sometimes commanded — and mourned even when right.
  • Deuteronomy institutes the bill of divorcement, framing all later Jewish divorce law. [C5]
      “When a man taketh a wife, and marrieth her, then it cometh to pass, if she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some unseemly thing in her, that he writeth her a bill of divorcement, and giveth it in her hand, and sendeth her out of his house,”
      — Deuteronomy 24:1 — The Holy Scriptures According to the Masoretic Text, trans. Jewish Publication Society (1917)
      Context: The Torah's divorce procedure: the get. What counts as an 'unseemly thing' divided Hillel and Shammai, and the debate frames all later Jewish divorce law.
  • The altar's tears record the tradition's grief at the lawful dissolution. [C6]
      [paraphrase — no public-domain translation quoted]
      Rabbi Eleazar said: whoever divorces the wife of his youth, even the altar sheds tears for him.
      — Gittin 90b — The Babylonian Talmud — Vilna edition, cited by folio; no public-domain English translation quoted
      Context: Divorce is lawful and the tractate regulating it is long — yet this closing word marks the tradition's grief at the lawful act.
  Note: The get remains in the husband's hand in traditional law, generating the agunah problem and modern rabbinic remedies — a live intra-tradition struggle.
  Further reading:
      - Judith Hauptman, “Rereading the Rabbis: A Woman's Voice” (1998) [book]
